1-1.text: Part one. What a fraction means. ... A fraction is part of a whole. The bottom number says how many equal parts there are. The top number says how many we have.

1-2.text: This pizza has 8 equal slices and 3 are shaded, so three eighths of it is shaded.

1-3.text: Fractions live on the number line too. Split 0 to 1 into 5 equal steps. The arrow points at three fifths.

1-4.text: Bars of the same length help you compare. Two thirds covers more than three fifths, so two thirds is bigger.

2-1.text: Part two. Equivalent fractions. ... One half, two quarters and four eighths look different, but they cover the same amount. They are equivalent fractions.

2-2.text: To make an equivalent fraction, multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. Two fifths equals eight twentieths, because both were multiplied by 4.

2-3.text: To simplify, divide the top and the bottom by the same number. Eighteen twenty-fourths: divide both by 6 to get three quarters.

2-4.text: A fraction is in its simplest form when no number except 1 divides into both the top and the bottom.

3-1.text: Part three. Fractions, decimals and percentages. ... Per cent means out of 100. Here 25 squares out of 100 are coloured, so that is 25 per cent.

3-2.text: One half, nought point 5, and 50 per cent are three ways to write the same amount.

3-3.text: To change a fraction to a percentage, make the bottom 100. Three fifths equals sixty hundredths, which is 60 per cent, or nought point 6 as a decimal.

3-4.text: These are worth learning: one quarter is nought point 2 5, which is 25 per cent. Three quarters is nought point 7 5, which is 75 per cent. One tenth is nought point 1, which is 10 per cent. And one fifth is nought point 2, which is 20 per cent.

4-1.text: Part four. Adding and multiplying fractions. ... When the bottom numbers are the same, add the tops: two sevenths plus three sevenths equals five sevenths. The bottom stays the same.

4-2.text: When the bottoms are different, make them the same first: one half plus one quarter equals two quarters plus one quarter, which equals three quarters.

4-3.text: Two thirds minus one quarter: twelfths work for both. Eight twelfths minus three twelfths equals five twelfths.

4-4.text: To multiply, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. Three quarters times two fifths equals six twentieths, which simplifies to three tenths.

5-1.text: Part five. Parts of amounts. ... To find three quarters of 20, divide by the bottom, then times by the top. 20 divided by 4 equals 5, and 5 times 3 equals 15.

5-2.text: 50 per cent is a half, so 50 per cent of 36 equals 36 divided by 2, which equals 18.

5-3.text: 10 per cent is a tenth, so divide by 10. 10 per cent of 45 pounds equals 4 pounds 50.

5-4.text: Build other percentages from 10 per cent. 30 per cent is 3 lots of 10 per cent: 3 times 4 pounds 50 equals 13 pounds 50. And 25 per cent is a quarter: 25 per cent of 80 kilograms equals 20 kilograms.
